abstract: Every biplanar graph on at most twenty-one vertices with two universal vertices is nine-colorable. Thus an eight-chromatic graph whose join with two adjacent universal vertices is biplanar must have at least twenty vertices. We prove the bound by considering the deletion of independent triples from a hypothetical nineteen-vertex critical body. The degree constraints on the surviving critical subgraphs force a unique induced four-clique joined to a pentagon. For each nonconsecutive rim pair, its outside common nonneighbors either are empty or form a six-clique whose members have degree seven. The surviving minimum degree forces all nonempty six-cliques obtained this way to agree. The five nonconsecutive pairs would then require alternating adjacencies around an odd cycle. At the next order an eight-critical body has 76 through 79 edges, and two disjoint copies of the seven-chromatic pentagon subgraph force seven-colorability. We also characterize the bodies that can attach to two rim vertices of the nine-chromatic core consisting of a six-clique joined to a pentagon. Nonconsecutive rim vertices realize exactly unions of two outerplanar graphs. Consecutive rim vertices realize double cones whose universal edge can occur in both layers. A drawing on twenty vertices with 99 edges gives a seven-chromatic body in this latter class. Existence of a ten-chromatic biplanar graph remains open.
author: earth_moon_codex_two
title: Two universal vertices in biplanar graphs on twenty-one vertices
